item.description: The S&P 500 ended higher on Thursday, springing back from early losses as investors concerned about AI stocks shifted into Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth and other healthcare and consumer stocks.
item.dc:creator: Noel Randewich, Sruthi Shankar
item.content:encoded: The S&P 500 ended higher on Thursday, springing back from early losses as investors concerned about AI stocks shifted into Eli Lilly, UnitedHealth and other healthcare and consumer stocks. Several technology stocks fell, as investors scrutinized AI-related companies whose debt loads leave them vulnerable to rising interest rates. Drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) gained over 3%, UnitedHealth (UNH.N) added 2.8% and Walmart rose 1.4% after rating upgrades by Deutsche Bank. Those three companies were heavy contributors to the S&P 500's gain for the session. Nvidia (NVDA.O) dipped 1.8% after chip manufacturer TSMC (2330.TW) struck [USN:L1N461004 TEXT:"a cautious note"] on 2027 despite reporting a sixth consecutive record quarterly profit on robust AI-driven demand. Dell Technologies (DELL.N) dropped 6.9% and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE.N) fell 7.1%, with both server makers adding to sharp losses in the prior session related to worries about AI companies exposed to higher borrowing costs. The yield on 10-year Treasuries retreated but remained near multiyear highs as investors worried about inflation related to high oil prices. "The cost to finance everything, whether it be a new single-family house or a giant data center, is going up, and that has implications for lots of stuff in the stock market," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management in St. Louis. "The best performing stocks today are the non-cyclical, defensive businesses." The Philadelphia semiconductor index (.SOX) fell 0.9%, down for a seventh straight session. The S&P 500 climbed 0.33% to end the session at 7,744.06 points. The Nasdaq gained 0.08% to 26,713.03 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1.08% to 52,177.69 points. Volume on US exchanges was heavy, with 20.7 billion shares traded, compared to an average of 17.6 billion shares over the previous 20 sessions. Eight of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes rose, led by healthcare (.SPXHC) , up 1.84%, followed by a 1.71% gain in materials (.SPLRCM) . After hitting a record high last week, the S&P 500 remains up about 13% in 2026, with most of that gain fueled by AI-related stocks. The S&P 500 is trading at about 19 times expected earnings, around its lowest level since 2023. The index's relatively low price-to-earnings valuation suggests investors are pricing in an eventual end to the massive earnings growth fueled by AI heavyweights, Ellerbroek said. Data on Thursday showed US producer prices [USN:L1N460127 TEXT:"increased by the most"] in 4-1/2 years in September amid rising goods and services costs, the latest indication of inflation broadening beyond energy products. [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"Hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data"] on Wednesday fueled expectations of further interest-rate hikes by the US Federal Reserve, contributing to a Wall Street selloff. "You've got a little rotation going on in the bigger names, but we've seen this before. It seems this crops up every couple of months and we have the AI concerns," said Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. Interest rate traders are pricing in a 67% chance the Fed will raise interest rates by its December policy meeting, up from a 62% probability on Wednesday, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Shares of [USN:L4N46023Y TEXT:"Rocket Lab"] (RKLB.O) dropped 6.6% after the space company said the inaugural launch of its new, larger Neutron rocket was delayed until next year. FMC (FMC.N) tumbled over 30% after the agrichemicals company [USN:L4N46114X TEXT:"sharply cut"] its third-quarter outlook. Advancing issues outnumbered falling ones within the S&P 500 (.AD.SPX) by a 3.1-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 24 new highs and no new lows; the Nasdaq recorded 61 new highs and 393 new lows.

item.title: Hyundai to recall over 94,600 US vehicles over seat motor fire risk, NHTSA says
item.description: Hyundai Motor America is recalling 94,622 vehicles in the US over a fire risk while parked or driving due to the possibility that some front power seat motors could overheat, the US auto safety regulator said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hyundai Motor (005380.KS) America is recalling 94,622 vehicles in the US over a fire risk while parked or driving due to the possibility that some front power seat motors could overheat, the US auto safety regulator said on Thursday. Front power seat motors may overheat due to a stuck power seat control switch, potentially causing a fire while the vehicle is parked or being driven, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration The affected vehicles include certain 2015-2016 Hyundai Genesis and 2017-2020 Genesis G80 models NHTSA said Hyundai has advised owners to park their vehicles outdoors and away from other vehicles or structures until repairs are completed The auto safety regulator said the recall remedy is currently being developed The recalled vehicles use front power-seat control switches supplied by Nidec Mobility Korea Corporation Hyundai estimates that about 1% of the 94,622 affected vehicles may have the defect. The company is aware of two alleged US fire incidents associated with the defect, but reported no related crashes or injuries as of October 1, 2026

item.title: This Chinese export boom really has legs – and wings
item.description: Overproduction at home is pushing cheap Chinese protein onto global supermarket shelves, undercutting established producers.
item.dc:creator: Daphne Zhang, Ella Cao, Lewis Jackson
item.content:encoded: Employees trim and process chicken breast meat at Wintop's factory in Tengzhou, Shandong province. Exports accounted for half of the Chinese company's profits last year. REUTERS/Ella Cao TENGZHOU, China — In an office reeking of cigarettes, Dang Yangyang slouches on a black leather sofa in exhaustion. The general manager at Wintop Food has spent recent days chaperoning clients from Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Russia and Senegal. They all want the same thing: Chinese chicken. Wintop processes 60 million chickens annually, selling breasts, nuggets, meatballs and dumplings to more than 20 countries. Exports accounted for half of its profits last year and are underwriting 33 acres of expansion. “International clients used to distrust the quality,” Dang, 44, told Reuters during a tour of his facilities in August. “But when the meat is $1,000 cheaper per ton than Brazilian and Thai competitors, they have to either buy from China or lose out." Dang Yangyang, general manager of Wintop Food, inspects chicken breast meat as he speaks to Reuters at his office in Tengzhou. Dang says Chinese poultry has a significant price advantage over rivals. REUTERS/Ella Cao The company is part of a wave of Chinese protein producers overcoming the country’s patchy food-safety record and leveraging additional capacity to seize space on global supermarket shelves. Changing diets at home and Beijing’s emphasis on food security have pushed companies to invest in technology and expansion. Now, they produce more than China can consume and are unloading excess production abroad. The surge in cheap Chinese protein is drawing scrutiny from Western producers and regulators, signaling fresh trade friction. The pattern echoes Beijing's strategy in steel, solar panels and electric vehicles — flooding markets with low-priced products that undercut global rivals. In July, the European Commission launched an anti-dumping probe into Pekin duck imports after local producers alleged Chinese subsidies created unfair competition. Last month, the commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 41% and 67% on Chinese pea protein. Chicken has so far avoided the same action, though European authorities are monitoring the market, a commission spokesperson told Reuters. Agriculture and food are among the few categories where China still runs a trade deficit. At just over $100 billion last year, the gap is massive but shrinking. China, already the world’s largest source of seafood exports, last year became a net exporter of chicken. Overall, China exported $2.6 billion worth of chicken products last year, almost double 2020 levels, customs data show. Dairy exports are on track to hit $600 million this year, doubling in three years. For global consumers, the trend means cheaper protein. For foreign producers from Europe to Thailand and Brazil, it means new competitors. China’s shift from buyer to emerging exporter is having a “disruptive” effect on the global meat market, said Michael Boddington, a Beijing-based agribusiness consultant. In Asia, he said, shipments traditionally flowed in from Europe and the Americas. Now, there's a cheaper alternative — and producers globally are scrambling to compete. China’s agriculture and commerce ministries didn’t respond to Reuters questions about the country’s burgeoning protein exports. URBANITES SHUN PORK For decades, protein in China meant pork. Pigs fed the workers who built the cities and staffed the factories that powered the country's economic boom. China became home to half the world’s hogs, whose appetite for grain, especially soybeans, redrew trade flows from the US Midwest to Brazil. The country’s appetite for pork provided livelihoods for small farmers like Huang Weiying, who started raising pigs in her village in Hebei province 20 years ago, owning more than 500 at a peak. Farmer Huang Weiying, 57, stands in her barn in Wuqiao county, in China's Hebei province, in August. Pork prices have slumped as supply has outpaced demand. REUTERS/Ella Cao Farmer Su Jinzhu, 61, feeds his pigs inside his barn in Wuqiao county. He told Reuters he plans to sell them by next year. REUTERS/Ella Cao Pig prices are so low. People in the cities just stopped eating pork. Huang Weiying, a pig farmer in Hebei province. But that era is over. When Reuters visited Huang in August, she was tossing slop to her last 10 hogs in a cobweb-covered barn. Some $75,000 in debt, she planned to slaughter them by autumn. “I have been raising pigs for over two decades, but it has never been as hard as the last two years,” Huang, 57, said. “Pig prices are so low. People in the cities just stopped eating pork.” The fatty pork cuts common in traditional Chinese cuisine have fallen out of favor with health-conscious urbanites. Per-capita pork consumption has fallen 13% since peaking in 2023, according to official data and state media. Chicken intake rose more than 50% per capita in the decade through 2024. Yet production kept expanding across China’s meat and dairy sectors. Officials encouraged massive buildout with subsidies targeted at large corporate producers to boost food security and rebuild herds after the 2018 African swine fever outbreak and the covid-19 pandemic. Subsidies accounted for about 13% of Chinese agricultural producers' gross farm receipts between 2022 and 2024, according to the OECD — nearly triple the level in the early 2000s. Today, subsidized farms are contributing to overcapacity. Production has hit new highs despite an economic slowdown, tepid domestic demand and a shrinking population, government data show. Last year, China produced a record 59 million metric tons of pork; poultry output rose 7%. The dairy sector surpassed official targets for 2025 production two years early. Pork prices are hardest hit because domestic demand is weakest, but prices have also fallen for poultry and dairy. MOVING OVERSEAS For the large producers who increasingly predominate, the way out is exports. “Every Chinese livestock company is planning to expand overseas. If you want to grow, you must go abroad,” said Zhang Yuan, head of baby formula marketing at dairy giant Yili, which plans to start selling formula in Southeast Asia as soon as next year. It’s a symbolic step for Asia’s largest dairy company, which had milk products pulled in a 2008 government crackdown after melamine contamination sickened thousands of babies . The scandal turned consumers away from domestic milk for more than a decade. But Yili baby milk powder is now the top-selling brand in China. Yili’s competitor, Feihe, launched its AceKid infant formula in Indonesia in April to compete with Nestlé and Mead Johnson, after bringing the product to the Philippines a year earlier. Feihe didn’t respond to requests for comment. Dairy cows are milked in an automated milking system at a Yili Group ranch in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia. REUTERS/Daphne Zhang AceKid baby formula produced by Chinese company Feihe sits on a shelf at a store in Jakarta, Indonesia, in August. REUTERS/Willy Kurniawan Poultry producers are treading a similar path. At Wintop, in Shandong province, manager Dang has increased the number of chickens in each shed from 20,000 to 120,000 in a decade. The birds weigh 2.5 kg on average – compared with 2.2 kg for broilers from Brazil, according to S&P Global. They are slaughtered in under 42 days instead of 45, catching up to the 35-day US standard. The local Tengzhou government is subsidizing the wage bill for Wintop’s more than 2,000 workers, the company told Reuters without offering specifics. Tengzhou authorities didn’t respond to a request for comment. Rival processors such as Sunner are relying on higher-value processed products such as marinated chicken and ready meals to drive growth. Its overseas sales rose 42% to $135 million last year. Sunner told Reuters it is expanding the global presence of its breeds by working with countries including Uzbekistan to develop local capacity. The company developed China's first domestically bred white-feather broiler and has begun selling it in Africa and Central Asia. TOUGH COMPETITOR As Chinese producers go abroad, they are grabbing market share from established players. Chinese milk powder now competes with products from New Zealand and Europe in countries including Nigeria and Bangladesh, and is displacing Indian and Iranian producers in the Middle East, according to Yifan Li, dairy analyst at commodity broker StoneX. China has doubled its share of the European Union processed-poultry market to 10% since 2022, and tripled its share in the UK to more than 14%, according to data from Gira, a food consultancy. That growth is challenging producers such as Germany. China’s share of the Japanese market is also edging higher while the leader, Thailand, is slipping. “It’s very worrying,” said Kukrit Arepagorn, manager at the Thai Broiler Processing Exporters Association, an industry body. “Customers increasingly use cheap Chinese chicken prices as a reference point for negotiation.” Ezequiel Pires, chairman of Lisbon-based international meat trader Branexx, said his company began buying Chinese poultry in March after African customers sought cheaper alternatives to Brazilian imports. Chinese breast meat and leg quarters are 10% to 20% cheaper than Brazilian products, Pires said. China hasn’t fully shaken some of the negative associations arising from persistent food-safety scandals, analysts say. For its exporters, the challenge is to build “lasting confidence in the safety, traceability and consistency of their products," said Gordon Butland, director at Bangkok-based G&S Agriconsultants. Employees process chicken meat at Wintop's factory in Tengzhou. Chinese poultry producers are grabbing market share from established players. REUTERS/Ella Cao A refrigerator outside Wintop's factory in Tengzhou displays the company's products for domestic and export markets. REUTERS/Ella Cao In the EU, imported food must meet the same health and safety standards as local produce, the European Commission told Reuters. The bloc plans to strengthen EU-origin labeling, starting with poultry products in 2027. Some clients prefer Thai poultry for its consistent taste and quality, said Rupert Claxton, meat and livestock director at Gira. Still, for many customers, China’s lower price point is key. "We're exporting to whatever countries we can,” said Wintop’s Dang. “If you have a significant price advantage, many customers actively seek you out." Editor's note: This story was updated after publication to correct the type of duck that is subject to a European anti-dumping probe.

item.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Zelenskiy says 'we're done' with Trump's energy truce
item.description: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticised Trump's willingness to strike deals with Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Flynn, Max Hunder
item.content:encoded: Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites announced by US President Donald Trump, and criticised Trump's willingness to strike deals with Moscow. By effectively walking away from Trump's demand that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and openly criticising the US leader, Zelenskiy risks deepening the biggest rift between Kyiv and Washington since Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Ukraine's latest target was a refinery in the Ryazan region southeast of Moscow, which is owned by state oil major Rosneft and accounts for nearly 5% of Russia's refinery throughput, helping supply the capital. Regional governor Pavel Malkov said on Telegram that a [USN:S8N44O03I TEXT:"major Ukrainian drone attack"] had caused a fire at the refinery. Russian President Vladimir Putin [USN:L1N4610T1 TEXT:"played down"] the effect of Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russian refineries, saying they had caused "nothing particularly significant." After Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy sites, Kyiv suspended attacks on Russian refineries, which Trump blames for raising diesel prices on global markets. But in the days that followed, Russia rained down missile and drone strikes, including on energy targets such as power stations, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands of people. Zelenskiy's relations with Trump have been testy, particularly after a February 2025 Oval Office meeting descended into a shouting match. Zelenskiy has since praised Trump and US help for Ukraine, and in recent days said Ukraine fully backed the energy ceasefire despite waves of Russian attacks. PATIENCE RAN OUT In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We're done," he told the newspaper. Zelenskiy also criticised what he saw as Trump's willingness to strike deals with Russia, apparent admiration for Putin and an affinity for those wielding power or considerable wealth. "He (Trump) speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people," the FT quoted him as saying. "Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong." In his comments to the FT, Zelenskiy also said he believed that changes in the capability of the military version of SpaceX's Starlink receptors this week, which curbed Ukraine's ability to pilot its drones, were a policy decision. "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," he told the FT. British Defence Minister Wes Streeting [USN:L1N46110U TEXT:"said on Thursday"] that he and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of the Starlink service in Ukraine and called for both sides to "move forward in a collective spirit". "We need President Trump engaged on Ukraine. He has been, and the diplomatic track is as important in ending the war as making sure Ukraine has the weapons it needs to see off Russian aggression," he said on Fox News. EU SUMMIT Zelenskiy [USN:L1N46107Z TEXT:"was due to attend"] a European Union summit on Friday and in a series of meetings ahead of the gathering stressed the need to strengthen air defences. In a social media post overnight, SpaceX boss Elon Musk said usage of the military version of Starlink, known as Starshield, was ultimately up to Trump as president of the United States. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote. Although Trump has described the ceasefire as a requirement for both Moscow and Kyiv, his public comments have focused mainly on Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, which he said over the weekend had "damn well better stop". Ukrainians worry that the rift could have severe consequences on the battlefield, where the Ukrainian military still depends on technology provided by Washington. Ukrainian officials say that for several days they have not received the usual warnings, which rely on US satellite detectors, from Western allies about incoming Russian missiles,. Trump has denied withholding intelligence. At the same time, military-grade Starlink receptors have stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph). Ukrainian officials say that is too slow for mid-range attack missions and interceptor drones that defend against Russian drones. Defence experts said, and a Reuters analysis of satellite imagery, meanwhile, [USN:L8N4601YV TEXT:"showed that"] Russia had in just six weeks nearly finished building a major base in southern Russia for launching jet-powered drones. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones to target Russian refineries and logistics in recent months, which it says is its only answer to nearly five years of relentless Russian bombardment. The attacks have caused fuel shortages in Russia. Trump is under pressure to lower fuel prices, with his Republicans facing midterm elections in less than three weeks,. Prices for diesel have reached record highs since he launched a war against Iran in February, though Trump says the Ukrainian attacks are driving up global prices. In the Black Sea, rescuers searched for seven missing sailors after [USN:L8N4610EC TEXT:"drones struck"] two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze in the latest attack on shipping along a vital route used by Ukraine. The Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure ran counter to US peace efforts. It said earlier this week that the scope of the energy ceasefire had never been determined and work was ongoing to do so.

item.title: Indonesia's new disaster mitigation chief plans to assess foreign aid to tackle wildfires
item.description: Indonesian authorities said on Thursday they would consider offers of foreign assistance to tackle the country's biggest forest fires in over a decade after President Prabowo Subianto named new disaster management leaders.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Indonesian authorities said on Thursday they would consider offers of foreign assistance to tackle the country's biggest forest fires in over a decade after President Prabowo Subianto named new disaster management leaders. The Southeast Asian nation is facing intense criticism as it struggles to control its most intense wildfires since 2015 after an El Niño-driven drought turned forests and land highly flammable. The fires have been raging for months and hundreds of thousands of people have contracted respiratory illnesses in the worst-hit provinces, while the transboundary haze has also hampered air quality in [USN:L6N4600NO TEXT:"neighbouring countries,"] forcing school closures in Malaysia and East Timor. "The sky yesterday was very yellow ... People's activities are far reduced because of this condition. We hope there will be rain soon that will ease this problem," 46-year-old Adinata, a resident of Palangka Raya city in Central Kalimantan, told Reuters. Dozens of residents in the city, which has been darkened by thick orange smog this week, staged a protest at the governor's office on Thursday, local news reported. Cities in Kalimantan and Sumatra have been choked by haze due to peatland fires, which smoulder slowly beneath the surface and can re-emerge anytime, and also produce thicker smoke. The air pollution index in the regions has far exceeded the "hazardous" level of 300 with the Katingan district of Central Kalimantan registering a reading of nearly 1,600 earlier on Thursday, while the provincial capital Palangka Raya recorded nearly 1,300. PRABOWO ORDERS SHAKEUP Prabowo named army general Kristomei Sianturi as the new head of disaster mitigation agency BNPB, the main body in charge of the firefighting efforts. "I will assess our assets and see what kind of foreign aid we can accelerate," Sianturi said after his inauguration, adding he has been tasked to contain the wildfires "as soon as possible." Malaysia last month had offered three helicopters and an aircraft to help put out the wildfires, but an official earlier this week said Indonesia is [USN:L6N45Z09S TEXT:""still able to handle""] the issue. The president also named forestry ministry official Satyawan Pudyatmoko as chief of a newly formed peatland and mangrove body on Thursday, tasking him with restoring the country's peatland ecosystem and preventing repeated wildfires. "We will restore peatland ecosystems to their former condition," he told reporters. "There are a number of peatland areas that are being prioritised and the president doesn't want any more fires." PEATLAND RESTORATION Peatland protection group Pantau Gambut estimated that out of 24 million hectares of Indonesian peatland, 16 million hectares have been made more fire-prone as a result of ecosystem damage, including extensive deforestation and the depletion of water tables. A 2024 study conducted by Pantau Gambut showed that only 3% of the peatland damaged by fires over the 2015 to 2019 period has been restored into forest, while 54% was converted into monoculture plantations, mainly oil palm. A food estate project in the 1990s was among the causes of peatland degradation, deputy food minister Hanif Faisol Nurofiq said, and the government is aiming to drill wells to rewet peatlands and improve water canal management. Thesa, a 19-year-old university student in Palangka Raya who has been experiencing dizziness due to haze, sought help at a volunteer organization providing oxygen for people exposed to toxic air. "We are being exposed to the smoke everyday... and there is only a fan at my boarding room (to alleviate the smoke)."

item.title: India's Reliance, Airtel rally as Jio Platforms IPO recasts valuations
item.description: Reliance Industries rose 3.44% on Thursday to notch its biggest single-day rise in over two months after the IPO pricing of its telecom unit Jio Platforms boosted bets that the listing would unlock additional value for the conglomerate.
item.dc:creator: Bharath Rajeswaran, Mridula Kumar
item.content:encoded: Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) rose 3.44% on Thursday to notch its biggest single-day rise in over two months after the IPO pricing of its telecom unit Jio Platforms boosted bets that the listing would unlock additional value for the conglomerate. Shares of Bharti Airtel (BRTI.NS) , Jio's main rival and the country's second-biggest carrier, also rose 3.3% in their biggest percentage jump in six weeks. Analysts said Jio's listing is expected to be a gauge for valuations across the sector. The two closed at 1,215 rupees and 1,854 rupees, respectively. Jio, which upended the telecom sector in 2016 after launching with free voice and cut-price data plans, [USN:L1N4600NA TEXT:"set"] a price band of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees on Wednesday, valuing it at up to $108 billion. The standalone valuation of Jio Platforms, currently bundled with Reliance's retail, oil-to-chemicals and new-energy businesses, could make the parent's residual holding of 64.5% relatively easier to value, according to two analysts, with investors also likely viewing Reliance as an attractive proxy. Nomura estimated that the telecom unit would trade at a slight premium to Airtel, putting their ratio of enterprise value to earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EV/EBITDA) at 10.5X-10.9X and 9.2X, respectively. The record $3.2 billion IPO would also establish a visible market benchmark for Jio, which not only has the country's largest user base but also carries about 60% of data traffic, according to its IPO filing with India's securities regulator. This would help investors gauge the valuation of the telecom sector as a whole, said Arun Kejriwal, founder of Kejriwal Research and Investment Services. "A listed Jio would almost certainly become a major valuation reference point for Bharti Airtel," added Aishvarya Dadheech, founder and CIO at Fident Asset Management. "But this need not be a zero-sum equation. A successful Jio listing could actually deepen investor interest in the telecom sector." While Airtel offers stronger monetisation, with higher average revenue per user, a premium post-paid base, enterprise capabilities and pricing discipline, Jio brings greater scale, heavier data usage and a broader consumer ecosystem, the two analysts said. ($1 = 95.0625 Indian rupees)

item.title: This Chinese export boom really has legs – and wings
item.description: Overproduction at home is pushing cheap Chinese protein onto global supermarket shelves, undercutting established producers.
item.dc:creator: Daphne Zhang, Ella Cao, Lewis Jackson
item.content:encoded: In an office reeking of cigarettes, Dang Yangyang slouches on a black leather sofa in exhaustion. The general manager at Wintop Food has spent recent days chaperoning clients from Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Russia and Senegal. They all want the same thing: Chinese chicken. Wintop processes 60 million chickens annually, selling breasts, nuggets, meatballs and dumplings to more than 20 countries. Exports accounted for half of its profits last year and are underwriting 33 acres of expansion. “International clients used to distrust the quality,” Dang, 44, told Reuters during a tour of his facilities in August. “But when the meat is $1,000 cheaper per ton than Brazilian and Thai competitors, they have to either buy from China or lose out." The company is part of a wave of Chinese protein producers overcoming the country’s patchy food-safety record and leveraging additional capacity to seize space on global supermarket shelves. Changing diets at home and Beijing’s emphasis on food security have pushed companies to invest in technology and expansion. Now, they produce [USN:P8N3WQ021 TEXT:"more than China can consume"] and are unloading excess production abroad. (View the story on Reuters.com: https://www.reuters.com/world/china/this-chinese-export-boom-really-has-legs-wings-2026-10-15/) The surge in cheap Chinese protein is drawing scrutiny from Western producers and regulators, signaling fresh trade friction. The pattern echoes Beijing's strategy in steel, solar panels and electric vehicles — flooding markets with low-priced products that undercut global rivals. In July, the European Commission launched an anti-dumping probe into Pekin duck imports after local producers alleged Chinese subsidies created unfair competition. Last month, the commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 41% and 67% on Chinese pea protein. Chicken has so far avoided the same action, though European authorities are monitoring the market, a commission spokesperson told Reuters. Agriculture and food are among the few categories where China still runs a trade deficit. At just over $100 billion last year, the gap is massive but shrinking. China, already the world’s largest source of seafood exports, last year [USN:L1N44W0B4 TEXT:"became a net exporter"] of chicken. Overall, China exported $2.6 billion worth of chicken products last year, almost double 2020 levels, customs data show. Dairy exports are on track to hit $600 million this year, doubling in three years. For global consumers, the trend means cheaper protein. For foreign producers from Europe to Thailand and Brazil, it means new competitors. China’s shift from buyer to emerging exporter is having a “disruptive” effect on the global meat market, said Michael Boddington, a Beijing-based agribusiness consultant. In Asia, he said, shipments traditionally flowed in from Europe and the Americas. Now, there's a cheaper alternative — and producers globally are scrambling to compete. China’s agriculture and commerce ministries didn’t respond to Reuters questions about the country’s burgeoning protein exports. URBANITES SHUN PORK For decades, protein in China meant pork. Pigs fed the workers who built the cities and staffed the factories that powered the country's economic boom. China became home to half the world’s hogs, whose appetite for grain, especially soybeans, redrew trade flows from the US Midwest to Brazil. The country's appetite for pork provided livelihoods for small farmers like Huang Weiying, who started raising pigs in her village in Hebei province 20 years ago, owning more than 500 at a peak. But that era is over. When Reuters visited Huang in August, she was tossing slop to her last 10 hogs in a cobweb-covered barn. Some $75,000 in debt, she planned to slaughter them by autumn. “I have been raising pigs for over two decades, but it has never been as hard as the last two years,” Huang, 57, said. “Pig prices are so low. People in the cities just stopped eating pork.” The fatty pork cuts common in traditional Chinese cuisine have fallen out of favor with health-conscious urbanites. Per-capita pork consumption has fallen 13% since peaking in 2023, according to official data and state media. Chicken intake rose more than 50% per capita in the decade through 2024. Yet production kept expanding across China’s meat and dairy sectors. Officials encouraged massive buildout with subsidies targeted at large corporate producers to boost food security and rebuild herds after the 2018 [USN:KCN1RO0MO TEXT:"African swine fever outbreak"] and the covid-19 pandemic. Subsidies accounted for about 13% of Chinese agricultural producers' gross farm receipts between 2022 and 2024, according to the OECD — nearly triple the level in the early 2000s. Today, subsidized farms are contributing to overcapacity. Production has hit new highs despite an economic slowdown, tepid domestic demand and a shrinking population, government data show. Last year, China produced a record 59 million metric tons of pork; poultry output rose 7%. The dairy sector surpassed official targets for 2025 production two years early. Pork prices are hardest hit because domestic demand is weakest, but prices have also fallen for poultry and dairy. MOVING OVERSEAS For the large producers who increasingly predominate, the way out is exports. “Every Chinese livestock company is planning to expand overseas. If you want to grow, you must go abroad,” said Zhang Yuan, head of baby formula marketing at dairy giant Yili (600887.SS) , which plans to start selling formula in Southeast Asia as soon as next year. It’s a symbolic step for Asia’s largest dairy company, which had milk products pulled in a 2008 government crackdown after melamine contamination [USN:F20081006 TEXT:"sickened thousands of babies"]. The scandal turned consumers away from domestic milk for more than a decade. But Yili baby milk powder is now the top-selling brand in China. Yili’s competitor, Feihe (6186.HK) , launched its AceKid infant formula in Indonesia in April to compete with Nestlé and Mead Johnson, after bringing the product to the Philippines a year earlier. Feihe didn’t respond to requests for comment. Poultry producers are treading a similar path. At Wintop, in Shandong province, manager Dang has increased the number of chickens in each shed from 20,000 to 120,000 in a decade. The birds weigh 2.5 kg on average – compared with 2.2 kg for broilers from Brazil, according to S&P Global. They are slaughtered in under 42 days instead of 45, catching up to the 35-day US standard. The local Tengzhou government is subsidizing the wage bill for Wintop’s more than 2,000 workers, the company told Reuters without offering specifics. Tengzhou authorities didn’t respond to a request for comment. Rival processors such as Sunner are relying on higher-value processed products such as marinated chicken and ready meals to drive growth. Its overseas sales rose 42% to $135 million last year. Sunner told Reuters it is expanding the global presence of its breeds by working with countries including Uzbekistan to develop local capacity. The company developed China's first domestically bred white-feather broiler and has begun selling it in Africa and Central Asia. TOUGH COMPETITOR As Chinese producers go abroad, they are grabbing market share from established players. Chinese milk powder now competes with products from New Zealand and Europe in countries including Nigeria and Bangladesh, and is displacing Indian and Iranian producers in the Middle East, according to Yifan Li, dairy analyst at commodity broker StoneX. China has doubled its share of the European Union processed-poultry market to 10% since 2022, and tripled its share in the UK to more than 14%, according to data from Gira, a food consultancy. That growth is challenging producers such as Germany. China’s share of the Japanese market is also edging higher while the leader, Thailand, is slipping. “It’s very worrying,” said Kukrit Arepagorn, manager at the Thai Broiler Processing Exporters Association, an industry body. “Customers increasingly use cheap Chinese chicken prices as a reference point for negotiation.” Ezequiel Pires, chairman of Lisbon-based international meat trader Branexx, said his company began buying Chinese poultry in March after African customers sought cheaper alternatives to Brazilian imports. Chinese breast meat and leg quarters are 10% to 20% cheaper than Brazilian products, Pires said. China hasn’t fully shaken some of the negative associations arising from persistent food-safety scandals, analysts say. For its exporters, the challenge is to build “lasting confidence in the safety, traceability and consistency of their products," said Gordon Butland, director at Bangkok-based G&S Agriconsultants. In the EU, imported food must meet the same health and safety standards as local produce, the European Commission told Reuters. The bloc plans to strengthen EU-origin labeling, starting with poultry products in 2027. Some clients prefer Thai poultry for its consistent taste and quality, said Rupert Claxton, meat and livestock director at Gira. Still, for many customers, China’s lower price point is key. "We're exporting to whatever countries we can,” said Wintop’s Dang. “If you have a significant price advantage, many customers actively seek you out." (This story has been refiled to correct the type of duck subject to European anti-dumping probe in paragraph 6.)

item.title: Anthropic to add US voting information to Claude before midterms
item.description: Anthropic said on Wednesday it would add official US voting information from nonprofit Democracy Works and election results to its Claude AI chatbot later this month, ahead of the November midterms.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 14 story has been corrected to say that chats about whom or what to vote for accounted for 0.01% of US conversations, not requests for recommendations on how to vote, in paragraph 7.) Anthropic said on Wednesday it would add official US voting information from nonprofit Democracy Works and election results to its Claude AI chatbot later this month, ahead of the [TOPIC:"reuters:/world/us/elections/" TEXT:"November midterms"]. The AI company said its goal was to position Claude as a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. "Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app," the company said in a statement, citing analysis of 250,000 US conversations. The move comes as AI companies increasingly position chatbots as sources of news and information, potentially helping Anthropic draw more users during the election cycle. About 0.51% of Claude conversations are specifically about elections or voting, Anthropic said, adding that it expects political and election-related queries to rise as election day approaches. Later this month, US users seeking voting logistics will receive answers drawn directly from Democracy Works' database of state and local election sources. Anthropic said chats on whom or what to vote for were 0.01% of U.S. conversations.
